**The new task X3-Y3-Z3 is not uniquely determined.** Two answer sets fit all the known tasks equally well. I give one of them, so confidence is about 0.5.

**Y components.**
- **Y2 = bit 2**, from X3-Y2-Z4 and X2-Y2-Z4.
- **Y3 = bit 4**, from X3-Y3-Z4: the answer depends only on whether the two bit-4 values match. This also fits X4-Y3-Z1.
- **Y4 = bit 3**, from X4-Y4-Z2.
- **Y1 = bit 1**, from X5-Y1-Z3.

**X3 and Z4.**
- In X3-Y3-Z4, button 1 appears exactly when the bit-4 values are the same.
- In X3-Y2-Z4, the same pattern holds on bit 2.
- So either X3 = "both are the same" and Z4 gives 1 when true and 0 when false, or X3 = "exactly one is 1" and Z4 gives 0 when true and 1 when false.
- X2-Y2-Z4 gives 1 when the bit-2 values differ. So X2 is whichever of those two rules X3 is not. Both choices stay consistent.

**X4.** It is "both are 1" or "not both are 1". Either way it fits X4-Y3-Z1 and X4-Y4-Z2, with Z1 and Z2 adjusted to match.

**X5 and Z3.**
- In X5-Y1-Z3, button 1 appears exactly when neither bit-1 value is 1.
- So either X5 = "neither is 1" and Z3 gives 1 when true and 3 when false, or X5 = "at least one is 1" and Z3 gives 3 when true and 1 when false.

**Combined assignments.** That gives 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 assignments. In every one, the X versions are all different from each other. For the new task they collapse to two outcomes:
- Matching bit-4 values give 1 and different ones give 3, or
- Matching bit-4 values give 3 and different ones give 1.

Nothing in the examples separates these two. I chose the first outcome: matching bit 4 → 1, different bit 4 → 3.

| # | Input | Bit 4 of each | Same? | Button |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0111 0001 | 1, 1 | yes | 1 |
| 2 | 0000 1111 | 0, 1 | no | 3 |
| 3 | 0011 0000 | 1, 0 | no | 3 |
| 4 | 1010 1011 | 0, 1 | no | 3 |
| 5 | 1110 0001 | 0, 1 | no | 3 |
| 6 | 0111 0111 | 1, 1 | yes | 1 |
| 7 | 0010 1111 | 0, 1 | no | 3 |
| 8 | 0001 0100 | 1, 0 | no | 3 |
| 9 | 0101 1110 | 1, 0 | no | 3 |
| 10 | 0000 1101 | 0, 1 | no | 3 |
| 11 | 1101 0000 | 1, 0 | no | 3 |
| 12 | 0001 0001 | 1, 1 | yes | 1 |
| 13 | 1110 0000 | 0, 0 | yes | 1 |
| 14 | 1001 0101 | 1, 1 | yes | 1 |
| 15 | 0100 1100 | 0, 0 | yes | 1 |
| 16 | 1110 0100 | 0, 0 | yes | 1 |

Under the other outcome, every 1 in the table becomes 3 and every 3 becomes 1.

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
